portfolio level, facilitating a structured approach to record information at different grades within the BE (Diagram 1, Fig. 1). The 
classification of the MPs in Waterman’s framework is presented as a pyramid. The material-level passport at the bottom of the pyramid 
details the properties and sustainability of individual materials. Moving upwards in the pyramid, the Component and Grouped 
Component Passports record how materials combine into building parts, while the Elemental Passport organizes data by building 
elements. The product-level passport is a result of grouping the material-level and component-level passport as a product consisting of 
various groups of components that can be sub-divided into single materials. The Building Passport aggregates all this information for a 
single structure. At the highest levels, Portfolio and Area-Level Passports offer a comprehensive view of materials and performance 
across multiple buildings or regions [65] (Diagram 1, Fig. 1).
Conversely, the BAMB project suggests a taxonomy of MPs categorized in “types” (diagram 2, Fig. 1) rather than “levels”[44]. This 
classification for MPs includes materials, products, and systems. Materials refer to raw, generic substances like metals, wood, and 
stone, which are described in product compositions but don’t have their own passports (Ingredient Passport). Products are manu­
factured items, like windows, doors, and tiles, that have specific properties and are sold on the market, each with its own MP (Product 
Passport). The systems are complex assemblies of multiple products, such as air conditioning or plumbing systems, where each part 
may have its own passport but together form a unified whole [5]. The ORMS MPs framework and policy [59], as is shown in diagram 
3 of Fig. 1, published in January 2024, also refers to MPs “levels” as types and is also based on Uniclass system (a. material, b. product, 
c. system, d. element and e. building passports). The lowest “level/ type” is the “Material” Passport for raw materials like glass or 
aluminium. These can be grouped into Product Passports (e.g., a glass panel) and further assembled into System Passports (e.g., a 
window). These systems can be integrated into broader Element Passports and ultimately contained within a Building Passport, of­
fering a structured yet flexible approach aligned with the Uniclass system used in BIM projects [59]. The ORMS classification for MPs 
offers a complementary perspective to Waterman’s and BAMB’s MPs frameworks, emphasizing the categorisation of similar charac­
teristics while maintaining independence from hierarchical structures [59]. This approach not only enhances the versatility of MPs 
frameworks but also promotes a more inclusive and integrated understanding of material flows and resource utilization within the BE.
In July 2024, it came into effect the “Eco-design for Sustainable Products Regulation” (ESPR-EU2024/1781), under the EU Circular 
Economy Action Plan [17], includes the creation of Digital Product Passports (DPPs). According to the new ESPR 2024/1781, DPPs are 
becoming a requirement and are intended to electronically store, process, and share product-related information among businesses, 
authorities, and consumers, promoting greater transparency and efficiency in the supply chain. Article 8 of the ESPR outlines the data 
and access rights related to the DPPs, ensuring traceability of products and components. The DPPs will be linked to a unique product 
identifier via a data carrier physically attached to the product or its packaging. The information must follow open, interoperable, and 
machine-readable standards and cover categories such as product description, materials, lifespan, performance, and sustainability data 
[19]. By definition, MPs are “digital datasets”, and material can theoretically be considered as “products”. Based on that, MPs are, in 
essence, DPPs, and future MPs frameworks should align with the ESPR 2024/1781.
